https://www.dw.com/en/india-student-ange.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IYSh Students have been protesting in Ranchi for over two weeks Image: Somnath Sen/ANI Advertisement Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process. Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly. The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters. The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi. Protesters clashed with police Monday as they marched towards the state parliament Image: ANI Video Grab In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led " Cockroach " protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike . Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated. "The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW. He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned. But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs. At least six protesters are on hunger strike in Jharkhand Image: ANI News/IMAGO What sparked the protests in Jharkhand? The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July. Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated. Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure. But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem. Devendra Nath Mahto has been on hunger strike for nine days and has lost more than 10 kilograms [FILE: August 4, 2026] Image: Somnath Sen/ANI What are the protesters' demands? The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated. They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery. The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies. The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken. "The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW. Anger at civil service recruitment exams in Jharkhand has been simmering for years Image: ANI Photo Has the Jantar Mantar playbook spread to the rest of India? The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers. That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan . CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters. But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined. Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi. "Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system ," Bora told DW. "They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future." Student leader Neha Bora (wearing glasses) joined the protesters in Ranchi Image: Yousuf Sarfaraz/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights. Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition. "Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW. "The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added. Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12. "The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment. India's Cockroach movement — and why it matters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Jharkhand's youth wants more from the Ranchi government The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media , hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession. The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission. But India's youth are refusing to stop there . Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure . For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest. "We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW. Photograph: Steven Saphore/AAP View image in fullscreen Emergency services were called to a Glen Alpine property in Sydney’s south-west at about 3.40am and found a man suffering from a gunshot wound, who died at the scene. Photograph: Steven Saphore/AAP Sydney Sydney home invasion during which man shot and killed a ‘targeted attack’, police believe Alleged offenders at large after man in his early 20s fatally shot in early hours of Tuesday Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Caitlin Cassidy Mon 31 Aug 2026 20.09 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 22.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man in his early 20s has been fatally shot in an alleged home invasion in Sydney’s south-west that police believe was a “targeted attack”. A homicide investigation is under way, with the alleged offenders still at large. Acting Supt Gretchin Atkins said the man, who was yet to be formally identified, was at his Glen Alpine home with his family in the early hours of Tuesday morning when multiple individuals allegedly broke in. Emergency services were called to the property at about 3.40am, Atkins said, where officers found the man with a gunshot wound. He died at the scene. Officers were told the unknown offenders fled the scene shortly before police arrived. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “We believe at this point in time it is a targeted attack – that is all the information that we’ve been able to gather at this time,” Atkins said. “Everything is certainly subject to our inquiries.” A crime scene has been established and an investigation is under way, with the assistance of the New South Wales crime command’s homicide squad. Atkins said police had confirmed there were “multiple” alleged perpetrators behind the attack but there was “a lot we don’t know”. “We are appealing to any person who was in the area, who saw, whether cars or people, who can assist us with our our current investigation, our inquiries,” she said. The victim was only known to police for a traffic offence, Atkins said, and otherwise had no known criminal involvement. She said his family were assisting with inquiries. Atkins also confirmed police were “aware” of reports of a social media post shared by an alleged Sydney gangland figure on Tuesday, claiming a shooting had been a case of mistaken identity. “A young man has lost his life today and that’s obviously just tragic,” she said. “There were family who were home and, as I said, they’re assisting us and being very, very helpful. “It’s an active crime scene and we’re obviously waiting for a lot of that information from our forensics who are on the scene.” The incident comes three days after a separate home invasion in Guilford where a 28-year-old man was fatally shot, also in the early hours of the morning. NSW police made no suggestion the cases were linked. It also follows the separate kidnapping murder of 85-year-old Chris Baghsarian earlier this year, who was abducted from his home in Sydney’s north in a case of mistaken identity. https://www.wired.com/story/kernel-panic.text: Welcome to Kernel Panic! A weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here. When every random text message feels like it’s a scam, and with AI supercharging digital fraud, old-time credit card skimmers and bogus letters that arrive in the mail may seem laughable as potential threats in 2026. But as we all suffer through a seemingly unending barrage of potential scams, these antiquated attacks are still costing victims around the world dearly. The fake-new-credit-card-in-your-mailbox trick is particularly insidious. Portugal, France, and Germany have all had waves of physical credit card scams in recent years where criminals have mailed phony replacement cards or letters to potential victims. Included letters often claim a current card is set to expire soon, whether the victim actually has one that's about to expire or not. In order for the new (fake) card to be activated, the scam letter says, it should be registered using an included QR code or URL. Some sham cards even have real customer names printed on them, says Georg Hauer, an adviser for digital banks. “The card is almost like a token that creates the trust that is needed in order to fall for the actual trick,” he says. If someone scans the QR code, they’re typically redirected to a fake banking website, where they’re asked to enter their details—potentially giving cybercriminals direct access to their real accounts. “This has been escalating for close to two years, and I believe that this type of scam might have proven to be successful enough to be rolled out in other countries,” Hauer says. “The cost of producing a personalized fake card has dropped in recent years thanks to AI just being able to copy a design based on an image, and the higher conversion rate per victim might justify the extra costs.” Mail scams aren’t the only ’90s throwback on the docket. The US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Alabama indicted two Romanian nationals last week on charges related to alleged credit card skimming. Authorities say the pair specifically targeted government SNAP food assistance benefits distributed to recipients in most states on antiquated magnetic stripe-only debit cards, or Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards. Fraud related to chip credit cards does exist as well, but this recent case serves as a reminder that classic skimmers targeting magnetic stripe credit cards are still deployed by scammers because there’s apparently still enough swiping going on to make it worth their while. The FBI says that EBT card skimming has risen in popularity among scammers since about 2021. “Skimmer fraud is rampant with losses in the United States alone reaching over $1 billion each year,” US Attorney Phillip W. Williams Jr. said in a press release about the recent indictment. (That billion dollars includes multiple types of credit card skimming, not just EBT targeting.) “It is a silent insidious theft that occurs by merely swiping a credit card at a point of sale.” Gary Warner, the director of intelligence at the cybersecurity firm DarkTower points out that dozens of states continue to use mag-stripe only cards for benefits purposes. “The risk here is that if the mag stripe is compromised, a clone of the card can be created and access not only the current value, but future value as well,” he says. More broadly, Warner tells us, there are still multiple risks related to making payments using the magnetic stripes on any cards—even if they also include more secure chips that have been issued over the last decade-plus. “Non-bank ATMs and smaller non-chain merchants may expose your chip-enabled card to mag stripe reading,” Warner says. “Mag-stripe skimmers are often installed in such a way that the chip read is forced to fail.” While magnetic stripe cards have gradually been phased out in the US over many years, they’re still around. Mastercard, for example, said last month that it will stop issuing any cards with stripes in 2029, and its remaining batch will be completely out of circulation by 2033. In the meantime, financial fraud has become one of the largest overall crime types in the US and around the world. Many attacks are focused on social engineering, mass phishing message campaigns, and other fraud where money ends up being sent by victims in transactions that often look legitimate to banks and other financial institutions. Hauer says criminals will always try to use methods that let them steal as much money as possible, even if that means sending physical letters in the mail. “The real idea behind some of these scams is to not essentially try to steal €2,000 from someone’s bank account, but rather actually empty a proper savings account, which holds much more money,” he says. If you feel like you’re already dodging scams left and right, there are some (relatively) easy takeaways to protect yourself from these old time scams. Avoid swiping cards whenever possible. And when you do need to swipe—as is, of course, the case with many EBT cards—do your best to check whether the terminal you’re about to use looks unusual, altered, or broken in any way. If so, use a different terminal. And apply the same skepticism that you have about texts and calls to letters as well. It feels like the only organizations that send mail these days are marketers, healthcare providers, banks, and the IRS, but scammers are still lurking there, too. Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at kernelpanic@wired.com. And stay safe out there.
